ai_summary: Great Britain’s total wind generation currently stands at 5.2 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output delivering 2.6 GW, which represents 25.7% of installed Scottish wind capacity. While Scotland maintains an optimal carbon intensity of 0 gCO2/kWh versus a significantly higher 201 gCO2/kWh GB-wide, severe north-south transmission bottlenecks prevent this abundant renewable power from serving wider demand centers. Consequently, a substantial 86.2 GWh of Scottish generation has been turned down through Balancing Mechanism bids so far today, incurring a direct constraint cost of about £2,912,375. To replace this blocked zero-carbon volume, fossil-fuel plants elsewhere were called upon to generate replacement power, burning an estimated 16,375,853 m3 of natural gas and releasing an avoidable 30,166 tonnes of CO2 into the atmosphere. Extrapolating today’s constraint volume across a full calendar year yields an estimated total yearly cost of curtailment of roughly £1,063 million. When socialized through balancing charges across national electricity demand, this level of curtailment is estimated to add approximately £3 to £4/MWh to everybody’s electricity invoice in the UK, highlighting the heavy economic and decarbonization penalties imposed by transmission constraints.
